settings.egarch: EGARCH(1,1) via arch.arch_model(vol='EGARCH', p=1, o=1, q=1); gamma[1] multiplies z(t-1) (signed term)
settings.egarch_E_abs_z: arch uses sqrt(2/pi) (normal) as centring constant; under Student-t this only shifts omega, not gamma
settings.reproducibility: deterministic optimiser, no random numbers used in estimation

quality.note: Suspicious observations are flagged, never deleted. Large |returns| (e.g. March 2020) are genuine market events.

return_validation.note: Log return differs slightly from simple % change by construction (ln(1+x) vs x).

adf.interpretation: The ADF statistic (-14.472) is below the 5% critical value (-2.863) with p = 6.578e-27. The unit-root null is REJECTED: the log-return series is stationary, so mean/variance models can be applied.

arch_lm.interpretation: Engle's ARCH-LM test with 5 lags on mean-equation residuals (r - mean): LM = 462.36, p = 1.058e-97. Null of no ARCH effects is rejected: conditional heteroskedasticity (volatility clustering) is present, which justifies GARCH-type models.

gamma_test.interpretation: EGARCH(1,1), normal innovations: gamma = -0.1460 (SE 0.0322, t = -4.54, two-sided p = 5.722e-06; one-sided p for H1 gamma<0 = 2.861e-06). Gamma is negative and statistically significant at 5%: negative standardised shocks raise next-period log variance more than positive shocks of equal size. This supports H1 within this model and sample.

forecast.note: QLIKE is robust to noise in the volatility proxy (Patton, 2011) and is computed with both the squared-return proxy and a high-low range proxy. Forecast accuracy is a different question from whether gamma is significant.

default_simulation.disclaimer: Model-implied experiment from estimated parameters. Not a market forecast.

nic_surface.note: Model-implied surface from estimated full-sample parameters (normal). Prior state m scales sigma(t-1) relative to the model steady state.

findings.hypothesis_decision: H0 REJECTED in favour of H1 (negative shocks have the larger effect) in the full-sample EGARCH(1,1)
paragraphs: Sample: 2725 daily log returns (2015-01-01 to 2025-12-31); mean 0.0422%, std 1.0267%, skewness -1.369, excess kurtosis 20.62; Jarque-Bera p = 0.
The ADF statistic (-14.472) is below the 5% critical value (-2.863) with p = 6.578e-27. The unit-root null is REJECTED: the log-return series is stationary, so mean/variance models can be applied.

Engle's ARCH-LM test with 10 lags on mean-equation residuals (r - mean): LM = 699.35, p = 8.651e-144. Null of no ARCH effects is rejected: conditional heteroskedasticity (volatility clustering) is present, which justifies GARCH-type models.
GARCH(1,1): alpha = 0.1037, beta = 0.8720, alpha+beta = 0.9757 (below 1 (covariance-stationary)); half-life of a variance shock about 28.2 days.

EGARCH(1,1), normal innovations: gamma = -0.0975 (SE 0.0200, t = -4.87, two-sided p = 1.131e-06; one-sided p for H1 gamma<0 = 5.657e-07). Gamma is negative and statistically significant at 5%: negative standardised shocks raise next-period log variance more than positive shocks of equal size. This supports H1 within this model and sample.

EGARCH(1,1), t innovations: gamma = -0.1047 (SE 0.0157, t = -6.65, two-sided p = 2.933e-11; one-sided p for H1 gamma<0 = 1.466e-11). Gamma is negative and statistically significant at 5%: negative standardised shocks raise next-period log variance more than positive shocks of equal size. This supports H1 within this model and sample.
caveats: Statistical significance is not economic significance: compare the size of gamma-implied variance differences with day-to-day volatility.
Lowest AIC/BIC shows relative fit, not that asymmetry is real or the hypothesis is true; the hypothesis is tested through gamma.
Differences in gamma across periods are only called significant when the formal Wald test says so (see robustness page).
The 2020 sub-sample has about 250 observations, so estimates are imprecise and may be sensitive to starting values.
A negative DAILY RETURN is not the same as a negative standardised INNOVATION z(t); EGARCH responds to z(t) = eps(t)/sigma(t).
Shock simulations are model-implied scenarios, not forecasts.
